lesson.title: A Wave Without Steps: Inside the Analog Signal
lesson.summary: An analog signal varies smoothly and continuously across an infinite range of values, which lets it represent sound and light naturally but also lets noise blend in undetectably.
lesson.body:
An analog signal is a signal whose value can vary continuously over time, taking on any value within a range rather than being restricted to a small set of fixed levels. Between any two points on an analog waveform, there are infinitely many possible values it could pass through, the same way a dimmer switch can set a light to any brightness level rather than just fully on or fully off. A temperature sensor that outputs a voltage proportional to the current temperature is a good non network example: the voltage can sit at any value across its range, not just a handful of preset steps.

Mathematically, a basic analog signal is often represented as a sine wave, written as amplitude times the sine of two pi times frequency times time, plus a phase term. Sound itself is naturally analog: air pressure varies smoothly as a wave, with no jumps between discrete levels. This is why early telephone systems, AM and FM radio, and older television broadcasts all used analog signals. They were representing an inherently continuous quantity, sound or brightness, with an electrical or radio signal that varied just as smoothly.

A concrete, everyday example is an FM radio station broadcasting at 101.1 megahertz. That number refers to the frequency of the station's underlying carrier wave, a continuous analog signal onto which the actual audio is encoded through a technique called frequency modulation, covered in more detail in a later chapter. The carrier itself, before any audio is added, is just a smoothly oscillating radio wave repeating 101.1 million times per second.

The defining weakness of analog signals is how they handle noise. Because any value along the continuous range is potentially a valid part of the signal, there is no way for a receiver, or an amplifier along the way, to tell the difference between the original signal and small amounts of electrical or environmental noise that get added to it during transmission. An amplifier used to boost a weakened analog signal over a long distance boosts the noise right along with it, since it cannot distinguish one from the other. Each amplification stage adds a bit more noise, and over a long path with many amplifiers, this accumulates, gradually degrading signal quality in a way that cannot be fully undone.

This noise accumulation problem is the central reason so many networks moved away from analog transmission over long distances, replacing telephone trunk lines, cable television backbones, and broadcast infrastructure with digital alternatives wherever practical. The next chapter looks at digital signals, which restrict a signal to only a small number of distinct values instead of a continuous range, and shows why that restriction, which sounds like it should carry less information, actually makes the signal far more resistant to exactly the kind of noise that degrades analog transmission.
